name: Bright Pink
lede: Bright Pink is a plain-English name for a vivid, slightly purplish pink, and the color belongs to the age of synthetic dyes; its best stories are about people who made it shocking, and one that is a myth.

sections.title: A descriptive name
sections.body: Bright Pink is a descriptive name, not a traditional one: our library takes this swatch from the xkcd color survey, and no older chart in it carries the name [1]. Who first used the two words as a color name is undocumented. Paterson's dictionary records the related *fiesta pink* as a bright pink, which shows the phrase working as a plain description [2].

sections.title: A color of the dye age
sections.body:
A pink this saturated is hard to make from old materials; compare the softer [[rose]] and the stronger [[magenta]]. The coal-tar dye eosin, a bright pink substance made from fluorescein, was marketed by BASF from 1874, after Hofmann worked out its structure [3]. Ball places it among the dyes that followed Graebe and Liebermann's synthesis of alizarin [3].

Earlier eras had their pinks too. Madame de Pompadour, the mistress of Louis XV, helped popularize bright pink Sèvres porcelain in the eighteenth century [4].

sections.title: Shocking pink
sections.body:
St Clair tells how the socialite Daisy Fellowes wore a bright pink diamond, the 17.47-carat Tête de Bélier, to meet the designer Elsa Schiaparelli [4]. Schiaparelli later wrote that the color was bright, impossible and impudent, a color of China and Peru and not of the West [4]. She used it for the packaging of her first perfume, Shocking, in 1937 [4].

In 1953 the costume designer William Travilla put Marilyn Monroe in a pink dress with a big bow for *Gentlemen Prefer Blondes* [4]. The painter-writer Derek Jarman claims that Christ's robe in Piero della Francesca's *Resurrection* is bright pink [5].

sections.title: The Baker-Miller story
sections.body:
A bright pink is also at the center of a famous myth. In 1979 Alexander Schauss reported that pink cardboard weakened young men, and on 1 March 1979 two naval officers in Seattle, Gene Baker and Ron Miller, painted a holding cell pink [6]. They stirred one pint of red trim paint into a gallon of white latex, and reported no incident in the next 156 days [6].

The claim that Baker-Miller pink calms aggression was never settled [6]. Later studies gave contradictory results, and a 1988 study found no link to blood pressure or strength [6]. It was also a paler pink, made with a little red in a lot of white, and not like this vivid swatch [6].

sections.title: Fluorescent pink
sections.body: Neon versions came later. On 21 April 1978 the punk band X-Ray Spex released 15,000 copies of a single called "The Day the World Turned Day-Glo", with a cover globe in poison-bright pink [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is #FE01B1, a screen color of unusual saturation (lightness 56, chroma 91 in LCH) [1]. We did not run an archive count for this exact swatch, so we make no claim about how often it appears in museum paintings. Any such count would be of photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not a pigment test.

questions.q: Did later studies agree that Baker-Miller pink calms aggression?
Which designer wrote that the shocking pink she saw on a diamond was a color of China and Peru, not of the West?

openers: A pink diamond gave Schiaparelli her signature color, and her first perfume was named Shocking [4].
Baker-Miller pink was made from one pint of red paint in a gallon of white, and later studies gave contradictory results on its calming power [6].

issues: Baker-Miller 'did not hold up' softened to 'never settled' (source: contradictory results)
Quiz and opener reworded to match
